transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Charles Snyder.
President Trump is back in Washington after wrapping up his latest campaign rally ahead of the November midterms.
He was in South Carolina to support Darlene Graham's U.S. Senate campaign.
He has to hold another rally tomorrow in Iowa.
Campaigning in Ohio, Vice President J.D. Vance weighed in on a controversial campaign ad in the race for governor.
From Member Station WVXU, Tanner Weingartner reports.
An attack ad from Republican Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign features the estranged mother of Democratic candidate Amy Acton,
accusing her of lying about several parts of her childhood, including a sexual assault.
The vice president said politics is a tough business and Republicans should focus on winning rather than choosing a side about a commercial.
Well, I'll be honest with you, whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern.
What is my concern is who's going to govern the next generation of American government.
Court records show Dr. Amy Acton's stepfather was charged with sexually assaulting Acton when she was 12 but never stood trial.
Acton says she hasn't spoken with her mother in nearly 50 years.
For NPR News, I'm Tana Weingartner in Cincinnati.
The top Democrats on the Senate and House Intelligence Committee say that while foreign powers are attempting to influence U.S. elections,
they have not seen evidence that any nation is trying to interfere in the voting process itself.
Here's NPR's Eric McDaniel.
Senator Mark Warner tells NPR that Russia, similar to prior occasions, is going after Democrats with misinformation.
He says Iran is looking more at disruption in Europe and that China has focused on local races or smaller issues with Chinese nationals involved.
The ranking intel member on the House side, Congressman Jim Haim, says that there is a profound distinction between those influence campaigns and actual interference in election infrastructure itself.
Haim also emphasizes that, quote, "We've never seen an operation to actually interfere, and as of now, we're not seeing either the capability or the intent to interfere."
Both men say they've told Trump's intel heads that they need to be reachable by phone and ready to provide evidence if the administration claims election fraud tied to foreign meddling.
Eric McDaniel, NPR News, Washington.
To the Supreme Court, the court says the Trump administration must continue to provide gender-affirming care to transgender inmates, as NPR's Jacqueline Diaz reports.
The Supreme Court's decision upholds a lower court's injunction on a federal bureau of prisons policy that would terminate hormone therapy and other treatments for trans inmates.
The court offered no explanation for the decision.
As a lower court's injunction remains in place, the litigation over the policy continues.
The American Civil Liberties Union sued the Trump administration over its proposed policy.
The organization believes there are more than 2,000 people in federal custody who identify as transgender and could be impacted by any future policy changes.
Jacqueline Diaz, NPR News.
And you're listening to NPR News.
The state judge has ordered tech giant Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook.
A New Jersey, rather a New Mexico jury, last month found Meta responsible for millions of violations of state consumer protection laws stemming from the Cambridge Analytica data harvesting scandal.
The fine imposed Wednesday is the biggest ever against Meta, which says it will appeal.
The threat of severe weather ongoing in parts of the southwest, the National Weather Service warning of the potential for flash flooding from excessive rainfall in northern and central Arizona through late Thursday evening.
Storms Wednesday brought golf ball sized hail.
New research offers some evidence that psychedelics may fight inflammation in people with diseases such as Parkinson's.
NPR's Will Stone reports on the findings published in the medical journal JAMA Psychiatry.
It's an area of psychedelic research that hasn't received as much attention, but experiments in animals consistently show some psychedelics have powerful anti-inflammatory effects.
Now a team at UCSF has published data from a small study of people with Parkinson's.
They saw markers of inflammation in the blood declined after they took psilocybin and that persisted 30 days after.
Dr. Ellen Bradley at UCSF says the findings need to be confirmed in larger trials.
This gives us this like initial biological signal to investigate.
People with neurodegenerative conditions are typically excluded from studies on psychedelics, but Bradley says they're finding these substances may actually help symptoms.
Will Stone, NPR News.
And I'm Giles Snyder. This is NPR News.

topics.text: Trump returns to Washington after South Carolina rally backing Darlene Graham's Senate campaign
Vance defends Ramaswamy's attack ad against Amy Acton, saying the ad's propriety is not his concern
Court records show Amy Acton's stepfather was charged with sexually assaulting her at age 12
Senate and House Intel Committee Democrats say foreign powers are influencing elections but not interfering with voting
Supreme Court upholds injunction requiring Trump administration to keep gender-affirming care for transgender inmates
New Mexico judge orders Meta to pay $25 billion over Facebook privacy deception
